0.title: Holy, Holy, Holy Is the Lord
0.overview:
Only one attribute of God is ever repeated three times in a row in Scripture. Scripture never says that God is "love, love, love" or "mercy, mercy, mercy." But twice, once in Isaiah's vision and once in John's, the creatures nearest the throne cry, Holy, holy, holy (Isa 6:3; Rev 4:8). And they never stop. Day and night, John says, they never cease to say it.

Holiness is not one quality of God among others. It describes everything he is. His love is holy love; his power is holy power; his justice, his mercy and his wisdom are all holy. To say that God is holy is to say that he is God, utterly unlike anything he has made, and utterly pure.

Our age has largely lost sight of this. God is often imagined as a helpful friend, a life coach or a kindly grandfather. He is kind beyond imagining, but he is never ordinary. And when the holiness of God fades from view, everything else fades with it. Sin seems small, grace seems unremarkable, the cross seems unnecessary, worship becomes casual and holiness of life seems optional.

The opposite is also true. When God's holiness comes back into view, everything changes. Sin is seen for what it is. Grace becomes amazing. The cross becomes the place where holiness and love meet. Worship becomes awe. And the call to be holy becomes not a burden but a privilege: to be made like the most beautiful being there is.

Six units: (1) What It Means That God Is Holy; (2) Holiness Revealed: Approaching a Holy God; (3) Holiness and Sin; (4) Holiness and the Cross; (5) Be Holy, for I Am Holy; (6) Worship and Glory: Holiness Forever. This study belongs with the studies on the Fear of the Lord and Biblical Wisdom. The holiness of God is why we fear him, and the fear of him is the beginning of wisdom.

1.title: What It Means That God Is Holy
1.overview:
At its root, to be holy means to be set apart. When Scripture calls God holy, it means two things above all.

First, God is set apart in majesty. He is the Creator, and everything else is creature. He is not the highest being on a scale that includes us. He is in a category of his own. After the Red Sea, Moses sang, Who is like you, O LORD, among the gods? Who is like you, majestic in holiness, awesome in glorious deeds, doing wonders? (Exod 15:11). Hannah prayed, There is none holy like the LORD: for there is none besides you (1 Sam 2:2). And God asks through Isaiah, To whom then will you compare me, that I should be like him? says the Holy One (Isa 40:25). The answer is no one.

Second, God is set apart in purity. He is perfectly good, without the smallest trace of evil, selfishness or deceit. Habakkuk says of him, You who are of purer eyes than to see evil and cannot look at wrong (Hab 1:13). His holiness is not merely the absence of sin but the fullness of goodness, a blazing moral beauty.

These two belong together. God's purity is not like ours at its best, only bigger. It is a different kind of purity, the purity of the One who is the standard of goodness itself.

And here is the wonder. This God, high and lifted up, does not stay at a distance. For thus says the One who is high and lifted up, who inhabits eternity, whose name is Holy: "I dwell in the high and holy place, and also with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit" (Isa 57:15). The Holy One draws near to the humble. In Hosea, God's holiness is even the reason for his mercy: for I am God and not a man, the Holy One in your midst, and I will not come in wrath (Hos 11:9). God is holy in his mercy as well as in his judgment. He does not forgive the way we forgive, grudgingly and partially. He forgives as God.
1.theology:
Holiness is God's Godness: Holiness is not one attribute on a list beside love, power and wisdom. It is the quality of all of them. God's love is holy, so it is never sentimental or indulgent. His power is holy, so it is never cruel or arbitrary. His justice is holy, so it is never vindictive.

The Holy One of Israel: Isaiah's characteristic name for God is the Holy One of Israel. It joins two ideas we might keep apart: God's infinite otherness and his covenant closeness. He is holy, and he is Israel's. your Redeemer is the Holy One of Israel (Isa 41:14).

The Holy Trinity: The Father is holy (John 17:11), the Son is the Holy One of God (John 6:69), and the Spirit is the Holy Spirit. Holiness is the shared life of the three persons of the one God.

Hallowed be your name: The first petition of the Lord's Prayer is hallowed be your name (Matt 6:9). Before we ask for bread, forgiveness or protection, Jesus teaches us to ask that God be treated as holy, in our lives and in all the world.
1.examples:
Then: When God first spoke to Moses from the burning bush, his first instruction was not about Egypt or Pharaoh. It was this: take your sandals off your feet, for the place on which you are standing is holy ground (Exod 3:5). Ordinary desert became holy because God was there. Moses' mission began with learning who God is.

Now: A Christian's mental picture of God has shrunk over years of busyness. Prayer has become a list of requests; Bible reading has become a quick devotional thought. Then, in a season of reading Isaiah slowly, he begins to see God's greatness and purity again. His prayers change. They start with adoration. His sins trouble him more and his forgiveness amazes him more. Nothing in his circumstances has changed. His view of God has.

A simple test: When you think of God, what is the first thing that comes to mind? If it is only what he can do for you, your picture of him is too small. Ask God to show you more of his holiness.

verseByVerse.quote: "Who is like you, O LORD, among the gods? Who is like you, majestic in holiness, awesome in glorious deeds, doing wonders? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: This song comes straight after the crossing of the Red Sea. Israel had just seen God's power and justice displayed. Their response is a question that expects the answer "no one": Who is like you, O LORD? God's holiness is his incomparability. The gods of Egypt had been humbled. The LORD is majestic in holiness, in a class of his own. Worship begins when we stop comparing God with anything else.

verseByVerse.quote: To whom then will you compare me, that I should be like him? says the Holy One. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Isaiah 40 is written to exiles who feel forgotten and small. God answers them not by making himself smaller but by showing how great he is. He measures the waters in his hand, calls the stars by name and holds the nations like a drop in a bucket. And then the question: To whom then will you compare me? The comfort of God's people is that their God has no equal. The one who cannot be compared is the one who gives strength to the weary (Isa 40:29).

verseByVerse.quote: For thus says the One who is high and lifted up, who inhabits eternity, whose name is Holy: "I dwell in the high and holy place, and also with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit, to revive the spirit of the lowly, and to revive the heart of the contrite. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: This verse holds together two truths that seem far apart. God is high and lifted up, he inhabits eternity, and his name is Holy. And he dwells with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit. The holiest being in the universe makes his home with broken, humble people. Holiness does not keep God away from the lowly. It keeps him away from the proud. The way into God's presence is down, not up.

verseByVerse.quote: I will not execute my burning anger; I will not again destroy Ephraim; for I am God and not a man, the Holy One in your midst, and I will not come in wrath. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Israel had been unfaithful again and again, and God had every right to destroy them. Yet he says, I will not execute my burning anger. Why? For I am God and not a man, the Holy One in your midst. Here holiness is the reason for mercy. A man, wronged so often, would give up. God is not a man. His holiness includes a covenant faithfulness and a compassion that go beyond anything human. The holy God is not only the one we must fear; he is the only one who can forgive like this.

1.reflection:
Before this study, what came to mind when you heard that God is holy? What would you add now?

Read Isaiah 40:12-31. Which description of God's greatness strikes you most, and why?

How does Isaiah 57:15 change the way you think about approaching a holy God?

What would it look like this week to pray "hallowed be your name" and mean it?

2.title: Holiness Revealed: Approaching a Holy God
2.overview:
The Old Testament teaches the holiness of God not only in words but in arrangements. At Mount Sinai, God told Moses to set limits around the mountain: Take care not to go up into the mountain or touch the edge of it (Exod 19:12). God was coming near, and his nearness was dangerous.

Then God gave the tabernacle, and its whole design taught holiness. There was an outer court, then the Holy Place, then, behind a thick curtain, the Most Holy Place where the ark of the covenant stood. And the veil shall separate for you the Holy Place from the Most Holy (Exod 26:33). Only priests could enter the Holy Place. Only the high priest could enter the Most Holy Place, and only once a year, on the Day of Atonement, and never without taking blood (Heb 9:7). Every curtain, every boundary and every sacrifice said the same thing: God is holy, and sinners cannot simply walk into his presence.

Two shocking stories reinforce the lesson. Nadab and Abihu, sons of Aaron, offered unauthorized fire before the LORD, which he had not commanded them, and fire came out from the LORD and consumed them (Lev 10:1-2). Later, when King David moved the ark on a cart, Uzzah reached out to steady it when the oxen stumbled, and God struck him down there because of his error (2 Sam 6:7). The ark was supposed to be carried by Levites on poles, as God had commanded (Num 4:15; 1 Chr 15:13-15). These events seem harsh to modern readers. But they teach that God is not to be approached on our terms. He must be worshipped as he has commanded.

All of this was preparing for something. The curtains and the blood were shadows. They pointed forward to the day when the true High Priest would offer the true sacrifice, and the curtain would be torn from top to bottom.
2.theology:
God sets the terms: Moses explained Nadab and Abihu's death with God's own words: Among those who are near me I will be sanctified, and before all the people I will be glorified (Lev 10:3). The closer people are to God, the more seriously they must take his holiness. Privilege brings responsibility.

Worship as God commands: The Old Testament repeatedly teaches that sincere intentions are not enough. Nadab and Abihu were priests; Uzzah meant well. God is to be worshipped in the way he has revealed, not in ways we invent. This is one reason Reformed churches have taken care to shape their worship by Scripture.

Holiness is contagious and dangerous: In the Old Testament, things that touched holy things became holy, and the unclean who came near the holy were in danger. The whole system of clean and unclean taught Israel that God's presence is not to be treated casually. When the men of Beth-shemesh saw what happened when the ark was mishandled, they asked, Who is able to stand before the LORD, this holy God? (1 Sam 6:20). It is the right question, and the gospel answers it.

Shadows of Christ: Hebrews says that the arrangements of the tabernacle showed that the way into the holy places is not yet opened (Heb 9:8). The curtain was a sign of separation, waiting for the one who would open the way.
2.examples:
Then: After Uzzah's death, David was afraid and angry, and he left the ark at the house of Obed-edom for three months (2 Sam 6:8-11). Then he learned. When he brought the ark to Jerusalem the second time, it was carried properly, with sacrifices, and David danced before the LORD with all his might (2 Sam 6:13-14). He discovered that reverence and joy are not enemies. Joy that knows God is holy is deeper, not smaller.

Now: A church wants to grow and begins to shape its services mainly around what visitors will enjoy. The music, the lighting and the length are all designed for comfort. Nothing is wrong with welcoming outsiders. But the elders begin to ask a harder question: is our worship shaped by what God has commanded and by who he is? They keep their warmth, and recover the reading of Scripture, confession of sin and prayer that reflect a holy God.

Now: A believer treats Sunday worship casually: arriving late, scrolling through a phone during prayer, singing words without thinking. Nothing dramatic happens. But Leviticus 10 still speaks: those who are near God must treat him as holy.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Nadab and Abihu, the sons of Aaron, each took his censer and put fire in it and laid incense on it and offered unauthorized fire before the LORD, which he had not commanded them. And fire came out from before the LORD and consumed them, and they died before the LORD. Then Moses said to Aaron, "This is what the LORD has said: 'Among those who are near me I will be sanctified, and before all the people I will be glorified.'" And Aaron held his peace. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Nadab and Abihu had been on the mountain with Moses (Exod 24:1, 9-11). They had seen God's glory. They were ordained priests. Yet they offered fire which he had not commanded them, and they died. Their sin was not that they worshipped too much, but that they worshipped on their own terms. Moses' explanation is God's own word: Among those who are near me I will be sanctified. And Aaron, grieving two sons, held his peace. Some truths about God are too weighty for an immediate reply.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they came to the threshing floor of Nacon, Uzzah put out his hand to the ark of God and took hold of it, for the oxen stumbled. And the anger of the LORD was kindled against Uzzah, and God struck him down there because of his error, and he died there beside the ark of God. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: To many readers Uzzah seems to have done something good. The oxen stumbled; the ark might fall; he reached out to steady it. But the whole procession was wrong from the start. God had commanded that the ark be carried by Levites, not loaded on a cart like Philistine cargo. Uzzah's reaching hand assumed that the holy ark needed rescuing by sinful hands. The story is not about a small slip. It is about a people who had grown casual about the presence of God.

verseByVerse.quote: but into the second only the high priest goes, and he but once a year, and not without taking blood, which he offers for himself and for the unintentional sins of the people. By this the Holy Spirit indicates that the way into the holy places is not yet opened as long as the first section is still standing (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Once a year, one man, with blood. That was the only way into the Most Holy Place. Hebrews says this arrangement was itself a message from the Holy Spirit: the way into God's presence is not yet opened. For centuries Israel's worship said, "Not yet." Every year the high priest went in and came out, and the curtain stayed in place. The whole system was waiting for a better priest and a better sacrifice, which the rest of Hebrews shows has come.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the men of Beth-shemesh said, "Who is able to stand before the LORD, this holy God? And to whom shall he go up away from us?" (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The men of Beth-shemesh had looked into the ark and been struck down. Their question is the great question of the Old Testament: Who is able to stand before the LORD, this holy God? They were right that no sinner can. But they asked it in fear, wanting God to go away. The gospel asks the same question and gives a different answer: no one can stand before God in his own righteousness, but those clothed in Christ's righteousness can stand, and even draw near with confidence.

2.reflection:
Read Exodus 26 and Leviticus 16. What did the tabernacle teach Israel about God? What does it teach you?

Why do you think God judged Nadab, Abihu and Uzzah so severely? How do these stories make you feel, and why?

How should Leviticus 10:3 shape the way we approach worship today?

David learned to combine reverence and joy (2 Sam 6). Which do you most need to grow in?

3.title: Holiness and Sin
3.overview:
The holiness of God is the measure by which sin is seen for what it is. When we compare ourselves with other people, we often look quite good. When we compare ourselves with God, there is no comparison at all.

That is why Scripture's great encounters with God's holiness always end with people on their faces. Isaiah cried, Woe is me! For I am lost (Isa 6:5). Job, after God spoke from the whirlwind, said, I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you; therefore I despise myself, and repent in dust and ashes (Job 42:5-6). Ezekiel saw the glory of the LORD and fell on my face (Ezek 1:28). Manoah, after seeing the angel of the LORD, said, We shall surely die, for we have seen God (Judg 13:22).

Sin is not merely breaking rules or failing to reach our potential. It is rebellion against the holy God. It creates a gulf: your iniquities have made a separation between you and your God, and your sins have hidden his face from you (Isa 59:2). And God's holiness responds to sin with wrath. For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men (Rom 1:18). God's wrath is not a loss of temper. It is the settled, righteous opposition of perfect goodness to evil. A God who did not oppose evil would not be good.

This is hard to hear, but it is necessary. If we do not understand God's holiness, we will think sin is small and grace is ordinary. We will treat forgiveness as something God owes us. But when we see God's holiness, we learn to say with Isaiah, "Woe is me," and that is the first step toward hearing, "your guilt is taken away."
3.theology:
Sin is against God: David, after his adultery and murder, prayed, Against you, you only, have I sinned and done what is evil in your sight (Ps 51:4). He had wronged others terribly. But the deepest offence of every sin is against the holy God.

All have sinned: for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God (Rom 3:23). God's holiness is the standard, and no one meets it. The respectable and the notorious alike need mercy.

Wrath is holy love's opposition to evil: Wrath is not the opposite of God's love. It is what God's holiness and love look like when they meet evil that destroys what he loves. A God indifferent to abuse, cruelty and injustice would not be loving.

Conviction is a mercy: When the Holy Spirit shows us our sin, it can be painful. But it is a sign of grace. Those who never feel the weight of sin never run to the Savior. God humbles us in order to lift us up.
3.examples:
Then: Job had argued for chapters that he did not deserve his suffering, and in a sense he was right. But when God appeared and spoke of his own greatness, Job did not win the argument. He worshipped. Seeing God changed everything, not because God explained his suffering, but because God showed himself.

Now: A respectable church member has always thought of himself as a good person. He does not lie, steal or cheat on his wife. Then, through a series of sermons on God's holiness, he begins to see the pride beneath his respectability, his impatience at home and his coldness toward God. For the first time he understands why he needs a Savior and not just a moral example. It is the beginning of real joy.

Now: A teenager hears a friend say, "A loving God wouldn't judge anyone." Wisely, she answers that she would not want a God who ignored evil: what would that say about victims of injustice? Then she explains that God's holiness and love meet at the cross, where he judges sin and saves sinners at the same time.

verseByVerse.quote: You who are of purer eyes than to see evil and cannot look at wrong, why do you idly look at traitors and remain silent when the wicked swallows up the man more righteous than he? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Habakkuk is troubled. God's eyes are too pure to look at evil, so why does he seem to tolerate it? The prophet's question rests on a true foundation: God cannot look at wrong with approval or indifference. God does see evil; he sees everything. But he cannot look on it with favour. Habakkuk's struggle shows us that the holiness of God is the believer's confidence in a wicked world. Because God is holy, evil will not have the last word.

verseByVerse.quote: but your iniquities have made a separation between you and your God, and your sins have hidden his face from you so that he does not hear. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The people complained that God was not hearing their prayers. Isaiah answers that the problem is not God's hand or God's ear but their sin: your iniquities have made a separation between you and your God. Sin is not only a moral failure. It is a broken relationship. It hides God's face. The only remedy is one that deals with the sin, and Isaiah goes on to promise a Redeemer who will come to Zion (Isa 59:20).

verseByVerse.quote: I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you; therefore I despise myself, and repent in dust and ashes." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Job had known about God for years. He was a righteous man. But there is a difference between hearing about God and seeing him. When God spoke, Job's response was not pride but repentance. I despise myself does not mean Job hated himself in an unhealthy way. It means he saw himself rightly next to God, and turned from his complaints to worship. Real encounters with God's holiness always produce humility, and humility is the doorway to restoration (Job 42:10).

verseByVerse.quote: For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, who by their unrighteousness suppress the truth. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul begins his great explanation of the gospel not with God's love but with God's wrath. That is not because wrath is more important. It is because no one understands the good news until they understand the bad news. God's wrath is revealed from heaven, already seen in the way God gives people over to the consequences of their sin (Rom 1:24-28). And it is against all ungodliness and unrighteousness, both the sins against God and the sins against others. This prepares for Romans 3, where God himself provides the answer.

3.reflection:
Why do people who see God's holiness, like Isaiah, Job and Ezekiel, respond by falling on their faces?

How does comparing ourselves with other people hide the seriousness of our sin?

Is it hard for you to think of God's wrath as holy and good? Why or why not?

Read Psalm 51. How does David's view of sin reflect his view of God?

4.title: Holiness and the Cross
4.overview:
The deepest question of the Bible is this: how can a holy God welcome sinful people without ceasing to be holy? If he simply overlooked sin, he would not be just. If he simply punished sin, no one would be saved. The answer is the cross.

First, God sent his Son, who was himself perfectly holy. The angel told Mary, the child to be born will be called holy—the Son of God (Luke 1:35). Even demons recognized him: I know who you are—the Holy One of God (Mark 1:24). Peter later called him the Holy and Righteous One (Acts 3:14). He lived the holy life no one else had lived. He is holy, innocent, unstained, separated from sinners (Heb 7:26).

Then, on the cross, the Holy One took the place of the unholy. For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God (2 Cor 5:21). God's holiness was not set aside at the cross. It was fully displayed. Sin was judged in all its seriousness, and the judgment fell on the Son. Paul says this was to show his righteousness at the present time, so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (Rom 3:26). At the cross God is both perfectly just and perfectly merciful.

And when Jesus died, the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom (Matt 27:51). The barrier that had stood for centuries was opened, from God's side. Now, Hebrews says, we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus (Heb 10:19). The question of the men of Beth-shemesh, Who is able to stand before the LORD, this holy God?, has its answer. Those who are in Christ can stand, and more than stand. They can draw near.
4.theology:
Holiness and love meet: At the cross God's holiness is not softened by his love, and his love is not limited by his holiness. Both are displayed at full strength. The cross is the most holy and the most loving event in history.

Propitiation: God put Christ forward as a propitiation by his blood (Rom 3:25). Propitiation means the turning away of God's wrath by a sacrifice. God himself provided the sacrifice that satisfies his own holiness. He is not a reluctant God who must be persuaded to love us. He is the loving God who paid the price his holiness required.

Holiness given to us: Believers are not only forgiven; they are declared righteous in Christ and set apart as God's own. And by that will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all (Heb 10:10). In Christ we are already holy in God's sight, and that is the foundation of our growth in holiness.

Access, not distance: The torn curtain means that the holiness which once kept sinners away now welcomes them in through Christ. The way of approach is still through blood and a priest, but the blood is Christ's and the priest is Christ.
4.examples:
Then: On the Day of Atonement the high priest went behind the curtain with fear, carrying blood, and came out again. Every year it was repeated, because no sacrifice could finally take away sin. When Christ died, the curtain was torn and never needed to be passed again with animal blood. The work was finished.

Now: A believer struggling with guilt over past sin feels unable to pray. "How can I come to a holy God after what I have done?" The answer is not to pretend God is less holy, but to look at the cross. God's holiness has already dealt with that sin in Christ. Hebrews says to draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith (Heb 10:22). The holiness that once barred the way now guarantees the welcome.

Now: Someone asks, "Why did Jesus have to die? Couldn't God just forgive?" A wise answer begins with God's holiness. Forgiveness that ignored sin would make God unjust and sin unimportant. At the cross God forgave in a way that shows how seriously he takes sin and how much he loves sinners.

verseByVerse.quote: For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: This verse describes the great exchange. Christ knew no sin. He was the Holy One, without the smallest stain. Yet God made him to be sin, treating him as the sin-bearer and pouring out on him the judgment our sins deserved. And the result: that in him we might become the righteousness of God. His holiness is counted as ours. Our sin was counted as his. No other religion has anything like this, because no other religion has a God both this holy and this loving.

verseByVerse.quote: whom God put forward as a propitiation by his blood, to be received by faith. This was to show God's righteousness, because in his divine forbearance he had passed over former sins. It was to show his righteousness at the present time, so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: For centuries God had passed over former sins. He had not punished them fully. That might have suggested he was indifferent to sin. The cross answers that question. It shows his righteousness: God was never indifferent; he was patient, waiting to deal with sin once for all in Christ. So now he is just, because sin is punished, and the justifier of believers, because their punishment fell on Christ. The cross is where God's holiness and his grace are both vindicated.

verseByVerse.quote: For it was indeed fitting that we should have such a high priest, holy, innocent, unstained, separated from sinners, and exalted above the heavens. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The writer describes Jesus as the high priest we need: holy, innocent, unstained, separated from sinners. Israel's high priests had to offer sacrifices for their own sins first. Jesus did not. He is fully holy. Yet separated from sinners does not mean distant from them. He ate with sinners, touched lepers and welcomed the outcast. He was separated from sinners in character, not in compassion. That is the kind of holiness we need in a Savior, and the kind of holiness he is forming in us.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, brothers, since we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh, and since we have a great priest over the house of God, let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, with our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience and our bodies washed with pure water. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The Most Holy Place, once entered by one man once a year, is now open to every believer. We have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, through a new and living way that he opened through the curtain, that is, through his flesh. His torn body is the torn curtain. And so the call is not "Keep away," but let us draw near. The holiness of God has not changed. What has changed is that we come clothed in Christ.

4.reflection:
Why could God not simply overlook sin? How does the cross answer that problem?

Read Romans 3:21-26 slowly. What does it show about God's holiness and his love?

How does the torn curtain (Matt 27:51; Heb 10:19-22) change the way you approach God in prayer?

Is there any sin that makes you feel you cannot come to God? What does the cross say to that feeling?

5.title: Be Holy, for I Am Holy
5.overview:
God's holiness is not only something to admire. It is something he shares. but as he who called you is holy, you also be holy in all your conduct, since it is written, "You shall be holy, for I am holy." (1 Pet 1:15-16). Peter quotes Leviticus, where the same command appears again and again (Lev 11:44; 19:2). God's people are to reflect God's character.

Scripture speaks of our holiness in two ways. First, believers are already holy in Christ. Paul tells the Corinthians, you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God (1 Cor 6:11). God has set us apart as his own. That is why the New Testament calls ordinary believers "saints," which means holy ones. Second, believers are being made holy, growing day by day in likeness to Christ. For this is the will of God, your sanctification (1 Thess 4:3). The first is God's once-for-all act; the second is his lifelong work in us.

What does holiness look like? It is not a matter of strange clothes, withdrawal from society or a list of man-made rules. Leviticus 19, the chapter that says You shall be holy, for I the LORD your God am holy (Lev 19:2), goes on to talk about honouring parents, caring for the poor, paying workers on time, not slandering, not holding grudges, and loving your neighbour as yourself (Lev 19:18). Holiness is practical. It is purity in body and mind, honesty in business, kindness in speech and love in action.

And holiness is driven by grace, not fear of rejection. Paul appeals by the mercies of God (Rom 12:1). Titus says that it is the grace of God that trains us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live self-controlled, upright, and godly lives in the present age (Titus 2:12). We do not become holy to be accepted. We pursue holiness because we have been accepted.
5.theology:
Definitive and progressive: Reformed theology speaks of definitive sanctification, the once-for-all setting apart of the believer in Christ (1 Cor 6:11; Heb 10:10), and progressive sanctification, the lifelong growth in holiness by the Spirit (2 Cor 3:18). Both are God's work, and both involve the believer's active obedience.

Not perfection in this life: No believer becomes sinless before glory. John writes, If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves (1 John 1:8). Holiness is real growth, not a claim to perfection. The holiest Christians are often the most aware of their remaining sin.

The means God uses: Jesus prayed, Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth (John 17:17). God makes us holy through his word, prayer, the fellowship of the church, the Lord's Supper and even through discipline and suffering, that we may share his holiness (Heb 12:10).

Holiness is necessary: Strive for peace with everyone, and for the holiness without which no one will see the Lord (Heb 12:14). Holiness is not the ground of our salvation, which is Christ alone. But it is the evidence of it. Those who belong to Christ will grow, however slowly, in his likeness.
5.examples:
Then: Joseph, tempted daily by his master's wife, refused because sin would be against God (Gen 39:9). When she grabbed him, he ran. Holiness sometimes looks like quiet faithfulness, and sometimes it looks like running out of the room.

Now, in the body: A young man struggling with pornography installs accountability software, gives a friend permission to ask him hard questions, and fills his evenings with better things. He fails sometimes and confesses quickly. Over months the grip loosens. That is progressive sanctification: real, slow and by grace.

Now, in business: A small-business owner discovers she has been undercharged by a supplier for months. No one would ever notice. She calls them and pays what she owes. Leviticus 19 calls that holiness too.

Now, in speech: A woman realizes that her conversations often slide into gossip. She decides that when someone's name comes up, she will either say something good or say nothing. Holiness reaches the tongue.

Not separatism: A Christian family is tempted to withdraw entirely from their neighbourhood to avoid worldly influences. Instead they stay, guard their hearts and homes, and love their neighbours. Holiness is distinctness, not distance.

verseByVerse.quote: but as he who called you is holy, you also be holy in all your conduct, since it is written, "You shall be holy, for I am holy." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Peter grounds the call to holiness in two things: who called you, and who God is. As he who called you is holy, so be holy. The command reaches all your conduct: there is no area of life where holiness does not apply. And Peter quotes Leviticus because the call has not changed from the Old Testament to the New. What has changed is that Christ has redeemed us with his precious blood (1 Pet 1:18-19) and given us his Spirit. The command is the same; the power to obey is new.

verseByVerse.quote: "Speak to all the congregation of the people of Israel and say to them, You shall be holy, for I the LORD your God am holy. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: This chapter is the heart of Leviticus' teaching on holiness, and it is surprisingly earthy. After the call to be holy, it speaks of parents, sabbaths, harvests left for the poor, honest weights, justice for the deaf and blind, respect for the elderly and love for the foreigner. And at its centre is you shall love your neighbor as yourself (Lev 19:18), which Jesus called the second great commandment. Holiness is not withdrawal from people. It is loving them as God loves.

verseByVerse.quote: And such were some of you. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul has just listed sins that exclude people from God's kingdom, and then says, And such were some of you. The Corinthian church included former idolaters, thieves, drunkards and the sexually immoral. But something had happened: you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified. All three are past tense. Before they had grown at all, God had already made them his holy people in Christ. That is the foundation for growth. We become in practice what God has already made us in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Strive for peace with everyone, and for the holiness without which no one will see the Lord. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The writer joins peace and holiness: strive for both. And he gives a sobering reason: without which no one will see the Lord. This does not mean we earn heaven by holiness. It means that the people who will see God are people God has made holy, and that this holiness will show itself in their lives. The verse is also a promise. One day the holy people of God will see the Lord. Every step of holiness now is preparation for that sight.

5.reflection:
What is the difference between being holy in Christ (1 Cor 6:11) and growing in holiness (1 Thess 4:3)? Why do we need both?

Read Leviticus 19. Which of its practical commands most challenges you?

Why is it important that holiness is driven by grace rather than fear of rejection?

Where is God calling you to grow in holiness right now: body, mind, speech, money, relationships?

6.title: Worship and Glory: Holiness Forever
6.overview:
The holiness of God is not only a truth to understand or a standard to live by. It is a beauty to worship. Worship the LORD in the splendor of holiness; tremble before him, all the earth! (Ps 96:9). Holiness has splendour. It is not cold and grey but radiant and glorious.

Psalm 99 is a hymn to God's holiness, and it rings with a refrain: Exalt the LORD our God; worship at his footstool! Holy is he! (Ps 99:5). And it ends, for the LORD our God is holy! (Ps 99:9). Worship is the right response to holiness. When we see God as he is, we cannot help but praise him.

In Revelation 4 John is taken into the throne room of heaven, and what he hears is the song of the living creatures: Holy, holy, holy, is the Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come! (Rev 4:8). They have been in God's presence longer than anyone, and they have not grown tired of his holiness. They never cease to say it. God's holiness is inexhaustible. Eternity will not be long enough to explore it.

And the end of the story is a holy people in a holy city. But nothing unclean will ever enter it (Rev 21:27). That sounds like a warning, and it is. But for believers it is a promise. Every sin that troubles us now will be gone. Christ will present his church holy and without blemish (Eph 5:27). And even ordinary things will be holy. Zechariah saw a day when there shall be inscribed on the bells of the horses, "Holy to the LORD." (Zech 14:20). Once only the high priest's turban carried those words. In the end, all of life will be holy to the Lord.
6.theology:
Holiness is beautiful: We sometimes think of holiness as strict and joyless. Scripture speaks of the splendor of holiness. God's holiness is the most attractive thing there is, and the more we see it, the more we love it.

We will see him: we know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2). The hope of seeing God is the hope of being made fully holy. And John draws the practical conclusion: And everyone who thus hopes in him purifies himself as he is pure (1 John 3:3). The future shapes the present.

God finishes the work: he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ (Phil 1:6). The holiness God began at our conversion he will complete at Christ's return. Christ reconciled us in order to present you holy and blameless and above reproach before him (Col 1:22).

All nations will worship: Who will not fear, O Lord, and glorify your name? For you alone are holy (Rev 15:4). The holiness of God is the theme of the final song of the redeemed, from every nation.
6.examples:
Then: When the high priest served, he wore a gold plate on his turban engraved with the words "Holy to the LORD" (Exod 28:36). It marked him as set apart for God. Zechariah's vision takes those words and writes them on horses' bells and kitchen pots. The holiness once concentrated in one man and one place will one day fill everything.

Now: A mother of young children feels that her days are anything but holy: nappies, meals, laundry and noise. Zechariah 14 speaks to her. Ordinary things done for the Lord are holy to him. The kitchen pot can be a vessel of worship.

Now: A believer facing death reads Revelation 4 and 21. He knows he is not yet what he should be. But he also knows that he will see the Holy One and be made like him. He is not afraid. The holiness that once would have condemned him is now his hope.

This week: Read Psalm 99 or Revelation 4 aloud. Begin your prayers with praise for God's holiness. Sing a hymn about God's holiness and think about the words. Ask God to show you one area where he wants to make you more holy, and thank him that he will finish the work.

verseByVerse.quote: And the four living creatures, each of them with six wings, are full of eyes all around and within, and day and night they never cease to say, "Holy, holy, holy, is the Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come!" (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The four living creatures are full of eyes all around and within. They see everything. And what they see, day and night, moves them to one unending cry: Holy, holy, holy. They are not bored, and they are not repeating a formula. Each time they look at God, they see more of his holiness, and so they say it again. Heaven's worship is not a ritual that grows stale. It is endless discovery of the infinite beauty of God.

verseByVerse.quote: Worship the LORD in the splendor of holiness; tremble before him, all the earth! (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Two responses sit side by side: Worship and tremble. And the setting is the splendor of holiness. Holiness is splendid. It is the most beautiful thing in the universe. The right response to beauty this great is both joy and awe. This psalm also calls all the earth to worship. God's holiness is not a private matter for Israel or the church. Every nation is called to bow before the Holy One, and one day every nation will.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, we are God's children now, and what we will be has not yet appeared; but we know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is. And everyone who thus hopes in him purifies himself as he is pure. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: John's hope is breathtaking: we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is. The sight of God will complete our transformation. And this hope is not merely future. Everyone who thus hopes in him purifies himself as he is pure. Those who expect to see the Holy One begin preparing now. Holiness in this life is the rehearsal for eternity. It is learning to love now what we will love forever.

verseByVerse.quote: And on that day there shall be inscribed on the bells of the horses, "Holy to the LORD." And the pots in the house of the LORD shall be as the bowls before the altar. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: In Zechariah's vision of the last day, the words once engraved on the high priest's golden plate are written on horses' bells, and ordinary cooking pots are as holy as the temple's sacred bowls. The division between sacred and ordinary disappears, not because holiness becomes common, but because everything becomes holy. That is the destiny of God's people and God's world. Every part of life, work, home, rest and play, will be Holy to the LORD.

6.reflection:
Have you thought of God's holiness as beautiful? What difference does the phrase "the splendor of holiness" make?

Read Revelation 4. What does the endless worship of heaven teach you about God's holiness?

How does the hope of seeing God (1 John 3:2-3) motivate you to pursue holiness now?

What ordinary part of your life could you offer to God as "Holy to the LORD" this week?
